questions.stem: Which pair of approximate percentages by volume correctly describes nitrogen and oxygen in dry air?

options.text: Nitrogen about 80 percent, oxygen about 20 percent
options.explanation: Nitrogen takes roughly four-fifths of the volume and oxygen one-fifth, which are the two figures of record for dry air.

options.text: Nitrogen about 20 percent, oxygen about 80 percent
options.explanation: That swaps the two shares; oxygen is the smaller fifth, not the larger four-fifths.

options.text: Nitrogen about 50 percent, oxygen about 50 percent
options.explanation: Air is not an even split; nitrogen dominates with four times the volume of oxygen.

options.text: Nitrogen about 78 percent, oxygen about 21 percent of the atmosphere
options.explanation: Those are the finer real-world figures, but the specification's approximate figures of record are 80 and 20 percent; quoting four-fifths and one-fifth is the expected answer.
options.misconception: precision beyond the approximate figures of record

questions.stem: Which gases make up the small remainder of dry air after nitrogen and oxygen?

options.text: Carbon dioxide, water vapour and the noble gases
options.explanation: These occupy the small leftover fraction of air, each present in proportions far below the oxygen fifth.

options.text: Hydrogen and helium in equal shares
options.explanation: Hydrogen is not a significant component of today's atmosphere, and helium is only one of the trace noble gases.

options.text: Chlorine and bromine vapours
options.explanation: The halogens are far too reactive to persist free in air; they appear in the atmosphere in no measurable share.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide in small amounts
options.explanation: Those are pollutant gases from combustion and traffic, not the natural fixed components of dry air.

questions.stem: What does the note say about how the composition of the atmosphere has behaved over time?

options.text: It has changed very little in 200 million years
options.explanation: The proportions of the main gases have been remarkably stable across that span, which is why approximate figures still hold.

options.text: Oxygen has steadily replaced nitrogen
options.explanation: No such replacement has occurred; the four-fifths and one-fifth shares have persisted.

options.text: Carbon dioxide has always been one of the two main gases
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide sits in the small remainder today; nitrogen and oxygen are the two main gases.
options.misconception: trace gas promoted to major gas

options.text: The composition was completely different before humans appeared
options.explanation: Over the 200-million-year window the mixture has stayed close to today's, long before humans existed.

questions.stem: Why is carbon dioxide described as significant despite its tiny share of air?

options.text: Because it has a substantial role in global warming as a greenhouse gas
options.explanation: A very small volume fraction can still absorb and store heat energy, which is what makes its warming role large.

options.text: Because it makes up about half the air by volume
options.explanation: Its share is tiny compared with the nitrogen and oxygen fifths; the significance is chemical, not volumetric.

options.text: Because it is needed for respiration in animals
options.explanation: Animals respire using oxygen and release carbon dioxide; the gas's atmospheric significance comes from heat trapping.
options.misconception: biological role substituted for climatic role

options.text: Because it gives air most of its mass
options.explanation: Nitrogen and oxygen dominate the mass of air as well as its volume; carbon dioxide contributes little.

questions.stem: A student claims dry air is a compound of nitrogen and oxygen. What is the correct verdict?

options.text: Wrong: air is a mixture, since its gases keep their own properties and only their proportions are fixed approximately
options.explanation: No chemical bonds join nitrogen to oxygen in air; the gases are simply mixed, and the small components vary slightly with conditions.

options.text: Correct: the fixed percentages prove chemical bonding
options.explanation: Approximate proportions are a feature of mixtures over time; a compound would need fixed ratios set by bonds and a single formula.

options.text: Correct, because nitrogen and oxygen react to form air
options.explanation: Nitrogen and oxygen coexist uncombined in air; they react only under extreme conditions such as lightning.
options.misconception: mixture imagined as a reaction product

options.text: Air is an element because it cannot be separated
options.explanation: Air can be separated by fractional distillation of liquid air, and it is a mixture, not an element.

questions.stem: Why does the water level inside the bell jar rise during the experiment?

options.text: Burning phosphorus removes oxygen from the air inside, lowering the gas volume so water moves in
options.explanation: The oxygen becomes part of a solid oxide, the gas volume falls, and the pressure drop lets water rise to fill the space.

options.text: The burning heats the water and makes it expand upwards
options.explanation: Expansion would push levels down or out; the observed rise comes from gas being consumed, not from heating.
options.misconception: thermal expansion offered as the cause

options.text: The phosphorus dissolves into the water and draws it up
options.explanation: Phosphorus stays in the jar burning; nothing dissolving could account for a rise matching one-fifth of the air.

options.text: Water is produced by the burning and collects inside
options.explanation: Phosphorus oxide is a solid, not water; hydrogen would be needed to make water, and none is present.

questions.stem: What makes phosphorus a suitable reactant for this experiment?

options.text: It burns readily until all the available oxygen is used up
options.explanation: Complete use of the oxygen is essential, and phosphorus keeps burning until the supply inside the jar runs out.

options.text: It reacts only with nitrogen, leaving the oxygen untouched
options.explanation: The whole point is to consume the oxygen; a nitrogen reaction would measure the wrong gas entirely.

options.text: It is completely safe to handle in the laboratory
options.explanation: Phosphorus is toxic and hazardous; its suitability is chemical, and safety requires great care.

options.text: It produces extra gas that pushes the water level up
options.explanation: No new gas appears; the measured change is the disappearance of oxygen, which is what makes the maths work.

questions.stem: A metal such as iron can replace phosphorus in this style of experiment. What is common to both versions?

options.text: Both remove the oxygen from a fixed volume of air, and the volume change gives the percentage
options.explanation: Whether metal or non-metal, the reactant must tie up the oxygen and leave the volume loss measurable.

options.text: Both must burn with a flame to work
options.explanation: Iron rusts without any flame; slow oxidation inside the closed volume does the same job given time.

options.text: Both consume nitrogen as well as oxygen
options.explanation: Neither reactant targets nitrogen; the measurement depends on oxygen alone being removed.

options.text: Both must finish within a single lesson
options.explanation: Iron versions take days; the timescale is irrelevant to the measurement principle.

questions.stem: Why must the air volume in the experiment be fixed and sealed?

options.text: So that the measured fall in gas volume corresponds exactly to the oxygen originally present in that sample
options.explanation: A sealed, known starting volume is what turns the volume change into a percentage of the original air.

options.text: To stop the phosphorus from escaping
options.explanation: Containment matters for safety, but the design reason is the fixed volume that makes the measurement meaningful.
options.misconception: safety reason substituted for measurement reason

options.text: To keep the water from evaporating
options.explanation: Evaporation is minor here; the seal exists to define the air sample being measured.

options.text: To prevent the nitrogen from reacting
options.explanation: Nitrogen would not react anyway under these conditions; the seal defines the sample, it does not protect the nitrogen.

questions.stem: After the experiment, roughly what fraction of the original air volume should the water have risen to occupy?

options.text: About one-fifth, matching the approximate 20 percent of oxygen in air
options.explanation: The oxygen share of dry air is about one-fifth, so the rise should be close to a fifth of the starting air volume.

options.text: About one-half
options.explanation: Half would imply oxygen made up half the air, contradicting the known composition.

options.text: About four-fifths
options.explanation: Four-fifths is the nitrogen share; nitrogen stays in the jar and displaces no water.

options.text: The whole volume, as all the air reacts
options.explanation: Only the oxygen reacts; nitrogen and the trace gases remain gaseous, so the rise is partial.
